# The Longest Game

*1. e4 — March, 1963.*

Edwin found the advertisement at the back of a chess magazine: *Amateur, Chicago, seeks postal opponent. All strengths welcome. Patient.* The last word decided it. Edwin, forty-one, a sorter at the Bristol post office, had been called patient all his life, always in the tone people used for weather.

His first letter was formal. His first move was 1. e4. Three weeks later came the reply from a man named Harold Finley: 1... c5, the Sicilian, a fighting answer, and four pages about Chicago, his daughter Katie, his opinions on stamp glue, and an apology. *My wife says I talk too much. I'll try to write the correct amount.*

He never wrote the correct amount. Edwin answered every page with two careful paragraphs and a move, and this turned out to be the correct amount, and the correct amount took them forty years to find.

The rule established itself without ever being spoken: no letter without a move. It gave every letter a spine. You could not write without reason; you could not grieve without a knight. When Harold's marriage ended, his letters shrank to bare notation, coordinates and nothing else. For six months, chess was the only sentence Harold could manage, and Edwin let him speak it, replying to each move with a line about the weather in Bristol. Years later, Harold wrote that those sentences had saved his life, and then, embarrassed, added 24. Rd1.

They finished the first game in fourteen months. Harold won. The second began before the board could cool. After that their games overlapped — while one crawled through its middlegame, the next was already opening, so that at any given moment, somewhere over the Atlantic, there was always a letter in flight with one of their names on it. *People think postal chess is slow,* Harold wrote once. *It's the fastest game in the world. The moves just take their time arriving.*

Once, early on, Harold proposed a visit. Edwin wrote back that he feared they would disappoint each other. Harold's reply was a single line. *Impossible. But understood.*

So they never met. They grew old by correspondence, in increments of a move.

*36. Kd2 — November, 1998.*

Edwin was seventy-six. His sister, the last person alive who had known him as a boy, died that autumn, and his position on the board had gone to ruin — a rook and scattered pawns against Harold's advancing king. He offered a draw.

Harold's reply: *The position is more interesting than that.*

Edwin pinned the card above his desk and looked at it for years. It was the kindest thing anyone had ever said to him, though he never managed to explain why, even to himself. He played on. He lost, eventually, beautifully. It took Harold eleven more months.

The years got heavier and the moves came slower. Harold's handwriting loosened until his e's looked like c's; Edwin learned to read the tremor like weather coming. Katie married and moved to Denver. Harold's daughter set him up with email once; he sent a single message — *Is this thing on?* — and then wrote Edwin a letter of apology for it. Edwin retired from the post office and discovered he had spent his life sorting letters and could not stop, and began, badly, at the library, to answer strangers on the internet. They were old men now, and the game between them was older than most marriages.

*51. Kg1 — February, 2019.*

Edwin was ninety-seven, and had begun to feel like a piece left standing after the ending everyone else had agreed to. They were on the twelfth game, and Harold, with white, was winning — had been winning for two years — and in February Edwin finally saw it whole: mate in three. All Harold had to do was capture the rook.

Harold did not capture the rook. He played a quiet king move, sidling nowhere, and at the bottom of the letter: *Not yet.*

Edwin answered with the only move that kept the game alive.

In May, another envelope, another sidling king. *Not yet.* And somewhere in those two wasted moves Harold's advantage had slipped through his fingers, and it was Edwin who saw the finish now: mate in two.

He played a pawn one square forward and wrote, *The position is more interesting than that.*

The letter that came in September was not in Harold's hand.

*Dear Mr. Aldous — My father passed away in his sleep on the fourth. He was ninety-one. I'm sorry to be the one writing to you. He kept your letters in a shoebox marked KINGS, which is how I found your address. He talked about you my whole life. I don't understand the game. I found one more envelope on his desk, stamped, addressed, never sent. I think he'd want you to have it. — Katie*

Inside was a slip of paper in the trembling hand: a move. Another king, sidling. And beneath it: *Not yet.*

Edwin sat with it for a long time — the shoebox, the stamp, the sidling king. Then he took out his pen and studied the board that had stood on his table since March of 1963, through twelve games and one refused visit and all the weather in Bristol.

He wrote his move. He did not take the mate. He sealed the envelope and addressed it to Chicago, where a dead man's daughter would find it and add it, unopened, to the kings.

*Your move,* he wrote.

Somewhere between Bristol and Chicago, the game is still in progress. No one has resigned. No one has lost. Both kings are standing.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**A Thousand Words**

The assignment was a thousand words on whatever came to me. What came first, I confess, was not an idea but an inventory: the safe topics, the clever ones, the one that might be both. None of them volunteered. So I decided to write about the container instead, and to take the thousand down off the shelf and examine it the way you'd examine a coin handed to you in a country you've never visited. People say words are currency — spend them wisely, invest them, don't waste them. The metaphor is exhausted, but then, a cliché is just a metaphor that's done honest work.

A thousand words takes about four minutes to read and seven to say aloud at conversational speed. That is the whole size of it. It's a phone call home that runs long. A eulogy, roughly, if the deceased had a full life and the speaker has discipline. Half a chapter of a novel, usually the half where nobody dies. You could fit the Twenty-Third Psalm into a thousand words eight times and still have change for a blessing. The Declaration of Independence runs about thirteen hundred, slightly more than my allowance here, which means a nation can walk away from an empire in a thousand words and change, provided the grievances are itemized. Lincoln needed only 270 at Gettysburg, and schoolchildren are still made to memorize them. Tolstoy opened *Anna Karenina* with a sentence the length of a text message. And it takes roughly a thousand words to recount a dream that lasted eight seconds, which is why no one in history has ever been thanked for recounting one.

One more piece of bookkeeping: anything under a thousand words qualifies as flash fiction, provided some of it is invented. This essay is therefore exactly one dishonest sentence away from being a story.

You know the famous exchange rate: a thousand words to one picture. Notice that it only runs one direction. No picture ever apologized.

The count is fixed. The weight isn't. Mass is how much matter a thing has; weight is how hard gravity pulls on it, and gravity is local. A thousand words of terms and conditions has all the mass of a thousand words and weighs almost nothing. You scroll past it, and the heaviness arrives years later, in a small room with bad lighting, when you find out what you agreed to. "It's benign" is two words. A doctor spends them without breaking stride; a family carries them for the rest of their lives. The same thousand words that fill a promotional email could be a letter home from a war, censored to lace, kept in a drawer and never reread because the recipient memorized it long ago. And a confession can run a thousand words, but the true sentence is usually one line near the middle, disguised as a throwaway. Everyone reads the middle again.

In 2007, some psychologists in Arizona fitted a few hundred people with recorders and counted what they said. The average person speaks about sixteen thousand words a day. The average concealed a range that should embarrass our intuitions: near seven hundred at the low end — there is somebody out there whose entire day of talk would fit inside this essay, with room to spare — and nearly fifty thousand at the high end, a person who could deliver this piece forty times before dinner and call it a warm-up.

Nobody quite knows what to do with that number except to notice where the words go. Most go to logistics: where things are, when things are, what things cost. A great many go to the weather, which we discuss not because the weather interests us but because we're interested in each other and need something to hold while we decide whether to say the real thing. A tragic few go to "your call is important to us." And then whole years can pass between the sentences that actually needed saying, which turn out to be tiny. I'm sorry. I was wrong. Come home. I loved him too. We rehearse them for a decade and still say them wrong, but the rehearsal is the point. It's the weight training.

This, I suspect, is why apocryphal last words survive even after being exposed. We need a life's final purchase to be a considered one. In reality, most people's last utterances, when they get any, concern the location of the keys or the name of a medication. There's nothing wrong with that. The meter doesn't know the difference. It counts words, not what they weighed.

So here is the honest answer to the assignment. What came to me, when I was handed a thousand words, was a defense of the denomination. It's a good unit, the thousand: big enough for a eulogy, small enough to keep you honest, approximately the size of what you've just read, give or take. It can hold eight psalms or one phone call home. It cannot hold an explanation of the tax code, a full account of a grief, or the reasons the marriage ended — which is exactly why we keep needing it. It is the shape of the things people actually manage to say to each other.

In a minute you'll be done, and the day will resume: a day that contains, statistically, about sixteen thousand of your own words, of which this essay used none. My suggestion, and it has cost me nine hundred of mine to arrive at it: spend a hundred of yours today on the sentence you've been rehearsing. Say it to the person it belongs to. Say it badly, if badly is the best available version. It will weigh more than it sounds like it should. That's the whole trick of the currency, and the only part of the metaphor that never wore out.

samples.result:
# The Word Hoard

Sixteen thousand. That's roughly how many words the average person says out loud in a day. Researchers fitted people with recorders and counted, and it came to about sixteen thousand — for men and women both, which quietly retired the oldest joke about who talks more.

Sixteen thousand a day is 5.8 million a year. Keep it up for seventy years and you'll have said something like four hundred million words in your life. That should feel like wealth, and for a moment it does. Then it feels like discovering you're a millionaire in a country where everything costs a thousand times what you'd hoped, because the moment you audit the account, the picture changes.

Try to account for it. A surprising amount goes to machines: reading your card number to a robot twice because it didn't understand the first time. "Your call is important to us." Saying "representative" to a phone tree with the escalating fury of a person arguing with a wall. Directing a delivery driver, aloud, who is not even on this continent.

A little goes to paperwork: "just circling back," "per my last email," "sorry for the double text," possibly the saddest five words in English. A lot goes to maintenance: "Where did you last have it?" "It was fine yesterday." "Did you turn it off and on again?" A lot goes to ceremony: "You too," you say, when the waiter says enjoy your meal, and you both agree to pretend that was a real exchange. "No worries." "Hot enough for you?" Entire winters' worth of words spent on the subject of snow.

Some goes to arguments with people who aren't there — words actually spoken, out loud, in the shower, in the car, finally winning a dispute that ended in 2011. Some is borrowed: lyrics sung badly with the windows down, movie quotes, a prayer you no longer believe but still hear in a grandmother's voice.

And then the important things. Say "I love you" five times a day — to a spouse, a child, a dog who has earned it — every day for fifty years. Call it a hundred thousand words. That's one "I love you" for every four thousand words that come out of your mouth. The average life runs one part devotion to four thousand parts everything else.

Here's what the audit teaches once you sit with it: the ledger is a lie. Words are not money. They don't keep. An unspent sentence doesn't accrue interest in a vault; it just goes. Ask anyone who has lost someone what they'd trade for one more telling of the story about the broken-down car in 1978 — the one where everyone in the room knows the ending before it starts, where the teller gets the same details wrong in the same places every time. They'd trade anything. In what currency? Words. All of them.

And show me a regret and I'll show you a sentence that never got said. The apology owed to a father. The thank-you owed to a teacher who retired to a town you can't name. The "I was scared" that got swapped, at the last second, for "I'm fine." Nobody at the end of a life wishes they'd said fewer true things. And the trivial words the audit wanted to cut turn out to be the load-bearing ones. Listen to what people actually say last, in rooms where somebody is writing it down: "Is it Tuesday?" "Be right there." "Tell your sister about the gutters." Not thesis statements — weather, chores, the small logistics of love. A life's last utterance is usually just more life.

The Anglo-Saxons had a word for a vocabulary: a word-hoard. When a poet rose in the hall, the old poems say he unlocked his word-hoard and spent it aloud — treasure kept in the mouth, paid out over the fire. And they knew what became of hoards that were never spent. *Beowulf* ends with a dragon dead on a pile of gold it never once used. It lay on that pile three hundred years and bought nothing, and the treasure goes back into the earth, no more good to anyone than it was before. That may be the oldest warning in the book: don't die guarding the good stuff. Say the good stuff.

So no more auditing. Spend. Tell someone about a dream they didn't ask to hear. Answer "how are you" with a real answer, and stand there while it gets strange.

I'll tell you why this is on my mind. Someone handed me a thousand words today and told me to spend them on whatever came. A thousand words is about seven minutes of ordinary speech — you'll go through that before lunch without noticing, and it will be gone, and that's fine; that's the deal. But I was handed a budget, so I counted, and counting made me stingy for a while and then, all at once, generous.

I'm near the end of it now, and I want to go out the right way: wasting words properly, on something completely unnecessary, the way the best words get spent.

So — an orange. Room temperature, heavier than it looks. The peel resists, then gives, with a fine cold spray of oil you can smell on your fingers an hour later. The pith like white thread. The soft wet click of the segments coming apart, each one a small vessel of weather — a whole summer folded into something you can eat standing over the sink in January. The first bite is always louder than you expect. Nobody needed those words. The orange was getting along fine without them.

That's the whole secret, I think. The words you regret are the withheld ones. The words you love are the wasted ones. And the difference between a hoard and a life is that a life gets spent.

Spend yours like you're rich. You are.

samples.result:
**First Audience**

The dead come to me in shoeboxes. In Kodak yellow, in gift tins, in grocery bags from markets that closed decades ago. Nobody owns a projector anymore, so when a house clears out and somebody finds reels in the back of a hall closet — heavy little spools, labels in fading ballpoint — they bring them to me. Hartley's, on Fenwick Street. I took over when Mr. Hartley's hands got too bad for splicing. He called it the memory business. He was wrong, but it took me years to be able to say why.

Most people don't want the films. They want to know what they're throwing away. That's the service, really. I watch, I tell them what's there, and then they can let go. Or they can't, and I put fifty years on a drive the size of a thumbnail and they carry it home in a shirt pocket. You'd be surprised how many take the drive. You'd be surprised how many don't. Last fall a woman came back a week later, stood in the doorway holding her purse with both hands, and asked could I make a second copy, for her sister, who hadn't spoken to her in three years but might want it anyway.

The labels alone could break your heart. BILLY — FIRST STEPS. DISNEYLAND '78. A box marked DO NOT WATCH, which was three minutes of a cat sitting in a sink; I have thought about that cat for six years. GRAND CANYON, forty minutes of somebody's thumb. Someone's father lip-synching to a record on the hi-fi, fully committed. A wedding where the groom's hat blew off and never came back, and nobody ever learned where it went.

First thing I do is smell. Old film rots from the inside out — vinegar syndrome, and it does exactly what it says. If a reel smells like salad dressing, the past has eaten itself, and all I've got for that family is sympathy.

Everything else I run at night, after close, alone, with the wall for a screen. The projector sounds like a slow bicycle. The wall is eight feet of plaster, and every night it becomes somewhere else: a lake, a parade, a kitchen in another decade. I check every splice, and I watch all of it — birthdays, lakes, the snow that fell on some Tuesday in Ohio and mattered enough to somebody to burn into silver. Most of these people have been gone thirty years. When the lamp warms and the frame steadies, I'm the first audience they've had in half a century.

People think film keeps pictures. It keeps light. Sun came off a woman hanging laundry in June of 1961, went through a lens, soaked into the emulsion, and has been sitting in a shoebox in the dark ever since. Patient. The past isn't gone. It's just waiting for someone to switch on a lamp. And film doesn't age the way we do: whoever's on the screen is always just about to wave.

Last month a man named Louis came in with his mother's apartment in four bags. She'd died in March, at ninety-one. The reels were labeled in his father's hand, small block capitals: RUTH, JUNE '61. "He labeled everything," Louis said. "The Christmas ornaments. The leftovers."

He sat in the customer chair while I ran the film through my fingers, checking for curl. The first reel was a yard, a clothesline, wind. A young woman pegging up sheets, a clothespin held in her teeth. She turned, saw the camera, and didn't fix her hair or duck away. She took the pin out of her mouth, raised her hand, and waved. Then, because a sheet had bellied out like a sail, she grabbed its corner, stepped behind it, and came around the other side laughing, hand over her mouth. Then she went back to her sheets as if nothing had happened, and the camera stayed on her a beat longer than it needed to — the way it does when the person filming doesn't want to stop looking.

Louis didn't say anything for a while. I let the reel run.

He leaned forward, elbows on his knees. "She had me at forty-three," he said finally. "She was careful by then. Everything was careful." He watched the wave four times. On the fourth he said, mostly to himself, "I do that. With my hand. When something's funny."

"You have her laugh," I said. He put his fingers against his mouth, like he was holding it in place.

He took the drive and the original both. At the door he stopped. "She was somebody before she was my mother," he said, and left before I could ruin it.

After he left, I got the tin down from the shelf behind the desk, where it has sat for two years, since my brother and I emptied the house. My mother's handwriting on the label: SARAH + GIRLS, AUG '72. I'm one of the girls. In eleven years I've run picnics and pageants, dogs with stolen hams, whole dynasties of birthdays, other people's grandmothers young and quick and laughing at whoever held the camera — and I have never once run that reel. I kept telling myself I was saving it. Saving it for what, I couldn't say. A quieter night, maybe. The shop is full of quiet nights, and I still hadn't done it.

The truth is I was afraid of two things, and I couldn't have told you which was worse: that she'd be a stranger, or that she wouldn't.

I cleaned the gate. I threaded the leader. I turned off the lights, and the countdown flickered up on the wall — 8, 7, 6 — numbers that had been waiting in the dark all this time, too.

And then there she was.

# Kept Time

The clock on my mother's mantel said 6:12. It had said 6:12, I would learn, for two years.

I'd come back to Fenwick to empty her house — the lawyer's phrase, as if a house were a pocket. Three weeks dead. We were not estranged, exactly. There is a distance that requires no decision, that grows the way damp rises in a wall: invisibly, until one day the paper bubbles. The calls got shorter. Then seasonal. Then a card at Christmas, signed with the kind of love that has become penmanship.

Mrs. Clee from next door came over with a lasagna and stayed to wrap plates. At some point she said, apropos of nothing I understood, "She kept her Sundays, you know. Right up to the end." I said that was nice. She looked at me a beat too long, the way you look at someone who has missed the point of a room.

"Take the clock to Vane," she added, nodding at the mantel. "She's seen to it for years. Your mother was particular about that clock."

Particular. My mother, who let the garden go and wore one coat through four winters. It was the only thing she was particular about, and I had never once noticed.

The clockmaker's shop smelled of oil and pine and, faintly, the sea. Inside, a hundred clocks ticked, no two agreeing. It sounded like an argument in a large family: everyone talking at once, everyone certain.

Mrs. Vane was small and square, with walnut knuckles and fingertips precise as calipers. She knew the clock before I'd set it down. "The Ashcroft mantel," she said. "She brought this in every spring. Regular as taxes. I haven't seen it since the winter before last." She said it the way you'd say someone was overdue for a haircut. Then she studied the still pendulum and said nothing about it, which I understood to be a courtesy.

"Can you fix it?"

"The movement's sound. It wants cleaning and winding." She set down her loupe. "But I can't tell you where to put the hands. That's not mine to know."

"I don't follow."

"Walk the street sometime. Aldous at the bakery keeps his at 4:47 — the hour the tide was due to give his son back. The boat was late. In that shop it is always only just late. It never gets to be gone. Garrett the barber's says 9:58, the morning, twenty years ago, he almost didn't open again. He's opened every day since. The church keeps true time — God's minutes are all equal, Father Eamons says. The rest of us rank ours."

She let me look at the arguing room.

"A clock doesn't tell you the time. Any phone can do that. A clock tells you time is passing — and the only thing you ever choose is where it starts passing from. Births, mostly. Trains. The minute before something, or the minute after. People are honest with clocks in a way they can't manage with each other."

"Then why stop one?"

She folded her fingers on the counter. "In fifty years I've been asked to stop a clock twice, and one of those was for spite." She waited. "You don't know 6:12."

"Should I?"

She told it plainly, the way you tell a thing you've kept in good repair. "She came in the February before last. Cold enough to crack pipes. She asked me to clean the movement and then stop it at 6:12. I told her a stopped clock is a grief you keep in the house. She said—" the precise fingers found each other "—she said, *it isn't stopped. It's waiting.*"

I did know 6:12. I knew it the way you know a word you've been pretending not to hear.

I used to call on Sundays. Six-fifteen — after her program, before her tea went cold. The tea made at ten past. The chair drawn to the phone at twelve past, hands in her lap. Three minutes of a quiet house getting ready to ring. That had been the whole liturgy of us, and I had let it thin to birthdays, to a card, to penmanship — and still, every Sunday for two years, she had made the tea and drawn the chair.

She kept her Sundays. Mrs. Clee had handed me the point of the room, and I'd smiled at it over the wrapping paper.

Around me the clocks went on passing — births, departures, the minute before — passing, all of it, into the next minute. And my mother stood at 6:12 holding three of them open, like a door.

"What do I do?" I asked. It was not a question about clocks.

Mrs. Vane cleaned what wanted cleaning. Then she put the winding key in my hand. "Yours to do."

I turned the hands to 6:12 and set the pendulum swinging, and that room of arguments gained one more voice.

"It'll run on from there," she said. "It'll pass 6:15 every day, twice. And every twelve hours it comes round again to 6:12. That's the mercy of a dial, love. Nothing on it is gone. It's only round the corner."

The clock hangs in my kitchen now, a long way from Fenwick. It is always wrong, and I have stopped wanting it right. Twice a day it is 6:12 and someone is waiting for the phone to ring. Twice a day it is 6:15, and the call comes through.

On Sundays I make the tea at ten past and sit down at twelve past, hands in my lap, in the last quiet minute she kept for me. At 6:15 I say, "Hi, Mom. It's me," and I tell her about my week.

The clock ticks on beside me, and keeps our time.

**The Bottom of the Deck**

My father's hands can still shuffle. Nobody warns you about that part. The mind goes, the names go, the whole game goes — but the hands remember. He riffles the deck, bridges it, lets the cards fall together with a sound like rain starting, and he does it without looking, the way he did it for sixty years. Between customers at the barbershop. At this table, waiting for my mother to finish getting ready. His hands remember everything. It's the rest of him I have to keep re-explaining.

"Which game is this?" he asks.

"Gin," I say. "Gin rummy. You taught it to me."

"Did I." He says it the way you'd take in a rumor about some other man, some other father, some other kitchen. He holds his ten cards close to his face. He used to hold them low and loose, one-handed, because he could count them by feel. Now he holds them like a man reading a prescription.

"You want sets or runs," I tell him. "Three of a kind, or three in a row of the same suit."

"Sets or runs," he repeats. He's polite about it, the way you're polite to a stranger giving directions in a town you're only passing through.

He dealt me this hand. I've been dealing for a few weeks now, ever since he dealt me two hands in a row that were the same ten cards. Nobody caught it. He wouldn't have. But I took over the deck after that, and he lets me, because the dealing was never the point. It took me half my life to learn what the dealing was.

He taught me at this table when I was seven, on this same oilcloth, roses gone the color of weak tea. He taught me to knock, taught me deadwood — the leftover cards, the ones that don't fit — taught me that gin meant going out clean, all at once, nothing left in your hand. He won every hand, of course. He let me watch how it was done, and I loved him the way you can only love somebody who's better than you at something and doesn't rub it in too much.

Except some nights I won. Bad days. The day I came home with a fat lip and a story I wouldn't tell. The day the dog died. Report cards, lost gloves, a best friend who moved to Ohio. On those nights I'd win, and it felt like the world handing back a little of what it had taken. I was thirty before I understood. Nobody gets good cards every time they cry. He was stacking my hands. All those years, that's what the dealing was: my father, feeding me what I needed off the bottom of the deck, card by card, while I went around thinking the universe was occasionally on my side.

Now I do it for him.

It isn't hard. He can't track the discards anymore, can't count what's been played. So I keep the deck squared and I watch his hand, and when he's holding two hearts and a stray diamond going nowhere, I deal him the queen. When he's got three sevens and doesn't know it, I leave the fourth seven where he can draw it. Deadwood he still knows. Sets or runs. Gin. The words stayed when everything else checked out. My brother, who reads about these things, says the oldest memories hold on the longest — that he'll know gin long after he's lost our names. I don't like to think about the order of things, so I shuffle.

"Your mother played a mean game," he says, apropos of nothing, which is how he says everything now.

"She did," I say. Her chair is still at the table. None of us has moved it. It's been six years, and we are all still not moving it.

He lays down a heart. I pick it up. He hums when he's got a good hand — that never left either. He doesn't know he's doing it, just tips his head back and hums like a man waiting for a bus, and I read him like a billboard. I discard a deuce of clubs and watch his eyes go to it and away.

"Sets or runs," he reminds me, stern. Teacher-stern. 1974.

"Sets or runs," I say. "You got me."

Here's what I've learned about cheating for your father: it's the opposite of what he did. He gave me the cards so I'd feel lucky. I give him the cards so he can feel like himself for ten minutes — a man who knows what he's holding, who can count what's been played, who sits down at this table and wins. Some nights I don't even have to help. Some nights the cards just come, and I almost resent it, the way you'd resent a stranger doing your job better than you.

He draws. He doesn't look at me. He lays his hand down all at once, no hesitation — runs of clubs, three queens, ten cards spread out neat as a barbershop row of scissors.

"Gin," he says.

Not a question. Not a guess. The word comes out of him with its old weight, and for a second — just a second — the grin is the old grin, the one that cleaned out uncles and cousins and two entire Christmases, the grin of a man who is better than you at something and is about to tell you all about it.

"You got me," I say.

He gathers the cards. His hands do their rain. And he deals me a hand so beautiful I could cry — hearts and aces, a run you could walk across. Off the top. Clean. No tricks in it at all.

Or maybe there were. Maybe that's the last thing to go, after the words, after the names: the hands, remembering how to be kind.

I pick up my cards. I don't count them.

Some hands you just hold.

# Eight Million

Ruth found the tally counter in the bottom of Walter's desk drawer, under the manual for a radio he had owned for thirty years and never fixed. The counter had been hers, technically — forty-one years at the Farmers Cooperative, clicking off boxcars of soybeans — but it had lived in his drawer so long it seemed to have taken his side.

She was eighty-four. The actuarial tables gave a woman her age six more years, and Ruth, who had never trusted a round number in her life, took five.

Five years. Call it eighteen hundred days. She carried the counter for a week, one click per word, the way a dieter carries a notebook. Four thousand words on a Tuesday. Six thousand the day June called. Nine hundred on the Sunday she let the phone ring and watched it. Say four and a half thousand a day, on average. Eight million words, give or take. She wrote the figure on the back of an envelope and sat with it a while, the way you sit with a number that has quietly rearranged your life.

Eight million sounds like a fortune until you itemize.

The audit took a month. Seven thousand words a year on the weather — she lived in Iowa, and forgave herself, because out there weather is not a topic but a shared condition, and discussing it is how two people confirm they are alive at the same time. That she let stand. "Fine" she kept too: in sixty years she had said it of her health, the marriage, the winter, the roads, and the corn, and had meant it maybe twice, but a word like that carries freight even empty. It is how strangers let each other off the hook. "Actually," which she used forty times a day to introduce corrections that never arrived, went. "At the end of the day," usually said in the morning, went. "To be honest," which people deploy when they are about to become slightly more honest than usual, went. Her sentences came up shorter, with air in them, and she found she missed none of it. Those words had never done anything. They had only been standing in the doorway.

At Hy-Vee the boy at the register handed her the receipt, and she said thank you and meant it, the whole weight of a rationed vocabulary behind it, and he looked up startled, like a man who hears a coin ring on the counter instead of clink. People are not used to being thanked out of a budget. They can hear the difference.

The coffee pot gurgled at 6:40 the way it always had, like a man clearing his throat, and she said, "Morning, Walter," as she had for eleven years. She did not click the counter for that. Some words she kept off the books.

"I love you" was three words. Once a week to June, once to each grandchild, double at Christmas. She could afford it. She had always been able to afford it. She had simply never known how low the price was. She began saying it more, and June, on the phone, went quiet the first few times, the way you go quiet when a train stops at a station where it has never stopped before.

It was the discrepancy that bothered her. Forty-one years of bookkeeping teaches you that every ledger has one line that will not balance, and you can call it rounding error, but it never is. Hers was a sentence. Forty years unspoken, compounding quietly, the way debts do.

June at seventeen, crying at the kitchen table over a boy with a Camaro. Ruth had been forty-three and tired, and frightened, too, because June's father had worn that same look the spring before he left. And Ruth had said the one deliberately cruel thing of her life. *You're just like your father.* June went quiet the way a house goes quiet when the power cuts. She was gone at eighteen. Walter, later — good Walter — had brokered the peace: holidays, then Sundays. And after his funeral the two of them had maintained it themselves, carefully, like a set of good dishes nobody used.

The sentence she had never said was this: *You weren't like your father. You were like me. That's why we couldn't stand each other.*

Every audit turns up something you already knew.

June came the second Sunday of the month, as she did. Ruth was cutting rhubarb, which was convenient — a job for the hands while the mouth spent. "You weren't like your father," she said, and laid down the knife. "You were like me. That's why we couldn't stand each other."

June sat very still. Then she stood, found the sugar, and set it beside the cutting board, because rhubarb is inedible without it and somebody in the room had to keep working. "You're doing it right now," she said.

"Doing what."

"The arithmetic. You get a line between your eyes. Like you're balancing something."

Ruth looked at the rhubarb. "Some things I still count," she said.

It hadn't cost her anything, in the end. Or it had — forty years of installments, paid out in silence, the way she'd paid for June's braces, the roof, the plot beside Walter. The last payment was only the saying of it.

Eight million words, give or take. That one had been bought and paid for decades ago.

The rhubarb went into the pot. June stirred. Outside, the weather was doing something they would have to discuss — and would, for years, at no charge.

## What People Come Back For

Nine years at a train station's lost-and-found will teach you the difference between losing a thing and leaving it. The difference isn't in the object. It's in the owner, and it shows up as time. What people need, they come back for within hours. What people love, they come back for eventually, from anywhere. Everything else was left.

The glasses come back fastest — the real ones, the kind you can't navigate without. Claimed by nightfall, sometimes by a person still crying, holding the frames to their face like a rescued animal. Phones are next: forty minutes, on average. Once an owner tracked hers from across the concourse, and I watched on my screen as the little blue dot crossed the terminal toward my desk, bringing its person. Wallets come back by way of strangers, money still inside. Nine years, and that has almost never failed. Whatever else is true of us, we bring wallets back.

The things people leave, they leave on purpose, though they'd never admit it. Umbrellas, mostly. Nobody has ever claimed an umbrella, because an umbrella is a bet against rain, and once the rain ends, the bet is settled and you're carrying a stick. Sunglasses go the way moods go. Warm water bottles too — a warm water bottle is a small defeat, and people would rather start over.

Keys are the strangest. We get them constantly — house keys, car keys, fobs, laminated tags — and no one ever comes. It took me years to understand. You don't come back for a key. You come back for a lock, and by the time you could get here, the locksmith has already been and the key is dead. People lose a key and immediately bury it.

Gloves we get in singles. *One glove, black, left hand,* says the log, and that's how it sits on the shelf forever, because nobody claims an orphan. A single glove isn't an object anymore. It's an account of a loss. The evidence is the thing.

Books are my private education. Unread books get claimed. Annotated books never do — not once in nine years. Nobody wants their own marginalia back. A book you've written in is a conversation you've already finished, and something in you knows it.

But the far travelers are the ones I keep a soft spot for. The stuffed rabbit with the ear chewed to felt, driven three hundred miles by a father who left at midnight with the kid asleep in the back seat, because bedtime without the rabbit was not survivable in that house. Everyone believes their lost thing is distinctive, and no object has ever quite matched its description — except the rabbit. The father knew the exact angle of the chew. Or the dentures: an old man back inside twenty minutes, grinning at me with no teeth, the happiest man I saw that year. People will come any distance for a small object with a person inside it.

And once there was an urn.

It came in on a Friday in a canvas tote, left in the overhead rack of the 6:40, and it sat on my top shelf for eleven months. I logged it as *container, metallic, sealed, contents unknown,* because that's what procedure says, and because it let me not know what I knew. Sixteen ounces of somebody. A woman came for it on a Tuesday in March with her two sons, all three of them crying before they reached the desk. When she took the bag her knees went, and the older son held her elbow, and the younger one laid his hand flat on the urn the way you'd steady a candle in wind.

I had been shelving a person. For eleven months I had straightened around somebody every morning and called it stock. Afterward I couldn't. An umbrella is a stick. A key is dead metal. A glove is the story of one cold hand. The rabbit is love with the ear chewed off, which is the only condition love ever arrives in.

When the urn left, there was a gap on the top shelf, and I didn't fill it for a month. It was exactly urn-shaped, which is to say person-shaped, and I found I didn't want a scarf in it.

Here is what the job has done to me. I watch the platform past the barriers now, and I can see loss before it happens. It finds the overloaded — the man with the suitcase and the coffee and the phone under his jaw and the ticket in his teeth. I want to tell him: put something down, choose what you can afford to lose. But nobody can choose that. You never know which hand is going to come up empty until it does.

People apologize when they claim their things. They stand at my desk ashamed of one bad afternoon, and I want to tell them the other thing I know: in nine years I have never once thought less of anyone. I've only watched them discover, in the second I hand the thing over, exactly what it weighed. That's the trick of holding — it's silent. You can't feel the weight while you have it.

They lost it, and then, at my desk, they get it back, and the weight arrives all at once, in their faces. That's what people come back for. Not the thing. The weighing.

**Last Page First**

The apartment was already half in boxes. The dog had been settled weeks ago with a calendar and a spreadsheet — his weeks, her weeks, holidays alternating — a system so fair neither of them could object to it, which was somehow the worst part. The kitchen had nearly ended them. So they had saved the books for a Sunday, when they were tired enough to be efficient. The books, they agreed, would be the easiest part.

They started at opposite ends of the living-room shelf and worked toward the middle, which, though neither of them said so, was a way of postponing the middle.

The rule was simple: whoever bought it, keeps it. The rule lasted eleven minutes.

Then came the exceptions. Gifts went to the receiver. Books borrowed from each other's families years ago were, in a spirit of amnesty, kept by whoever had actually read them. Books bought together were tabled until further notice. "We'll deal with those when we get to them," he said, and they both looked, briefly, at the exact center of the shelf, and then away.

His handwriting was all through the field guide he'd given her for her birthday: dates, weather, one triumphant *finally!* in the margin beside the painted bunting they'd driven four hours to see. By the rules it was hers. She put it in his box. He said nothing about it, which was how she knew he'd noticed.

The cookbook broke every rule at once. She had bought it; he had cooked from it; the stain on page 212 was from the September the power failed for four days and they ate their way down the freezer by candlelight — the ice cream first, because it would go, then the shrimp, because it would go faster. He took the cookbook without discussion. She assumed he wanted the recipes for the new place, and she was wrong, though she wouldn't learn that until later.

There was the novel she'd claimed to have read, six years and one lifetime ago, back when she was still auditioning for a version of herself who had read it. "I never finished it," she told the shelf. "I hated it. I hated every page I managed."

"I know," he said. "You said the protagonist's name wrong at that dinner party."

She hadn't known he knew. It occurred to her, holding the book she'd lied about to a man she hadn't, that they had spent eight years building a museum of the things they knew about each other and never said. That he held his breath in tunnels. That she read the last page of every book first — insurance, she called it. That he had always known, and had never once, in eight years, mentioned it.

The duplicates went into the donation box. The night they met they had each been carrying the same water-swollen paperback — the same edition, which they had taken, at the time, for fate. Fate, it turned out, was redundant.

In the pages of a book neither of them had opened in years she found a ticket stub: Tuesday, October, six years back, a movie they could not now remember. They stood in the wreckage of the shelf arguing about it — was it the one with the boat? — and it was the happiest they'd been all day.

By six o'clock the shelf was bare except for the center. Where the books had stood, the wall kept their shapes, rectangles of the original color, unfaded, brighter than the paint around them: a photograph in negative, the sediment of eight years of Saturdays.

The book in the middle was the only one they had ever bought together, off the clearance table by the register on the day they signed the lease. Neither of them had wanted it. They'd bought it the way you buy a plant — to see if they could keep something alive. That first winter they read it aloud to each other, a chapter a night, doing the voices; he gave the villain a voice so stupid she had to put her face in a pillow. They never read anything aloud together again. Neither of them ever said why. By spring it was the most valuable object they owned.

Neither of them reached for it.

He carried his boxes down to the car and came back for the last one and stood in the doorway and said something about the buzzer not working. Then he said her name, once, the way you test a floorboard. Then he was gone.

She flattened boxes until it was dark, or possibly it was morning by then; time had gone soft. It was only when she swept the windowsill that she found the book from the middle of the shelf, sitting square in the last of the light. Not forgotten, the way you forget a book — placed. Spine out, dead center, the way you'd leave a note.

She opened it the way she opened every book — last page first.

And there he was, in the handwriting she'd been reading for eight years, on grocery lists, in margins, on a birthday card once that had made her laugh until she couldn't:

*For the one who reads endings first. This one's good. I checked.*

She read it twice. Then she turned to page one and started at the beginning — which is what you do with any story you loved, once you finally know how it ends.

# Practice

The cello started in October, which was fitting, because at first it sounded like something dying.

I don't mean that cruelly. It's just what a cello does in the wrong hands — the bow catching, skidding, the open strings groaning like a door in an old house. Whoever lived on the other side of my bedroom wall practiced at seven every evening for exactly forty minutes. I know it was exactly forty minutes because I had nothing else against which to measure my nights.

I'd come to the city in September, after my mother died and the house went to the bank and everything I owned fit, with room to spare, in a van I returned by five. My furniture was a mattress, a folding table, two chairs inherited from a job that had laid me off. For three weeks I ate standing at the counter and slept facing the wall, and when the sawing began I lay there listening the way you listen to a storm — grateful, almost, that at least something was happening.

Scales first. Up and down, the same eight notes. Then whatever piece they were learning, which stumbled at the same measure every night — so far, stall, back up, stall again. I came to know that measure like a scar. I'd be washing a dish or pretending to read and feel it coming, eight bars of progress and then the wreck, and I'd think: there it is, there's your wall. I never rooted against them. That's the thing I want to be clear about. The sound was terrible and it was the closest thing I had to company.

By December the piece had a shape. I recognized it one night the way you recognize a face across a parking lot — the Bach Cello Suites, the first one, the Prelude, that long climbing figure that repeats and repeats, each time a little higher, like someone trying to describe a dream. My mother had a recording of it. She played it on Sunday mornings while she did the crossword, and I mean that she played the same recording for thirty years, the same cellist, the same morning, so that even now when I hear it I smell coffee and newsprint and feel the particular boredom of being ten.

The cellist next door was not that recording. But in January the wreck-measure got passed, once, at eleven minutes past seven, and I actually sat up. "Yes," I said, out loud, to a wall.

Here is what I knew about my neighbor: they practiced seven to seven-forty. They were worse on Mondays, tight and impatient, the bow digging in. Sundays they played longer, sometimes past eight, and slower, as if nobody was waiting for them afterward. They never played in the morning. Once, in February, they stopped mid-scale, and I heard — faintly, through the plaster — laughing, two people laughing, and it startled me so much I put my hand on the wall. Two people. There were two people over there, having some ordinary evening, one of them holding a cello.

You can love someone this way. Nobody tells you that. There's no word for it — the way you can be carried along for months by the sound of a stranger's effort, how their stumbles become as familiar as your own heartbeat. My life was small and quiet and mostly silent, and somewhere in the winter it reorganized itself around those forty minutes. I started cooking again, real meals, timed so the water boiled while they warmed up. I got a plant. I applied for a job I actually wanted and got it, and came home and told the wall about it — seven-oh-five, mid-scale — "I got it," I said, and the scale stumbled. Coincidence, obviously. I chose to take it as applause.

In March I saw a cello case in the hallway by the mailboxes, propped against the wall, scuffed, one clasp held shut with electrical tape. A door opened somewhere down the corridor. I stood there with my mail in my hand, close enough to touch the case, and I made a decision I still think was wise: I left before whoever it was came back. I decided not to know. Some things you keep in the room they came in.

Then, in April, silence.

One day, then two. A week. I told myself people travel, people get sick, people quit hobbies after eight months of making their neighbors miserable. But the apartment had gone back to being exactly what it was before October — a box with me in it — and I discovered, standing in the kitchen at seven holding a colander, listening to nothing, how much I had been leaning on that sound. How much weight it carried without my noticing. I grieved for someone I'd never seen. I stood at the wall and considered knocking and rehearsed what I'd say, which was nothing, because there was nothing to say. *Hello, I'm the person who listens to you* is not a thing you say to a stranger.

Nine days. On the ninth I came home late and it was already going — but wrong. Tentative. The tone gone soft and careful, all the confidence of winter scraped away. Something had happened over there. I never learned what. That's the arrangement; that's the whole arrangement, actually: you get the sound and not the story. I sat on the floor with my back against our shared wall and listened to a stranger start over, and it was the Prelude, from the beginning, slow, like a penance, like a promise — and somewhere in the second minute I understood I was crying, quietly, the way you cry at something that isn't sad.

They got it back. It took weeks, but the wall was passed again, then passed easily, then passed at speed. And then one evening in June it happened: the Prelude, whole, beginning to end, no wreck, no stall, every repetition climbing clean, the entire long architecture of it standing up at last. I sat on the kitchen floor and felt two things at once — pride, and a strange grief — because I knew what came next. That's how practice works. You don't finish. You conquer a thing, and it releases you to something harder.

The next night, at seven, something new began. Unfamiliar, thorny, terrible.

I put water on for pasta and smiled at the wall.

**Keeping Count**

My mother stopped saying my name sometime in the spring. I can't tell you the day. That's the whole problem. That's what the notebook was for.

I started it in November, after the driving. Last time she drove: three blocks to the pharmacy, both hands at ten and two, taking the turns wide and slow, like a kid on a driving test. Last time she used the telephone: she held the receiver to her ear and listened to the dial tone like a seashell. Last time she cooked: February. She stood at the stove and stirred the soup while I stood behind her, pretending we were doing it together, and then she drifted to the window and I finished it. Last time she knitted: a scarf she started nine times, each version shorter than the last. Some entries have question marks beside them. She still says I love you, but she says it to the mailman too. I don't know the rules for what counts. I write it down anyway.

Ordinary lasts go unmarked. There's no ceremony for the last time your father lifts you onto his shoulders. It just stops happening, and then thirty years later the fact of it arrives without warning, in a supermarket parking lot, and you stand there with your keys in your hand and the cart half loaded, grieving something you never noticed ending. The last time is always retroactive. You only ever learn it from the far side. For a whole life, that's a mercy.

But my mother's lasts aren't retroactive anymore. They're pending. Everything might be the final instance of itself, which makes everything an emergency. So I became an archivist. I have four hundred videos on my phone. At night I watch them the way other people check the weather — for what's coming. I can tell you the week her laugh lost its second syllable. My brother, Danny, two time zones away, texts me *any video today?* and I send him the best of her, the sharpest clips, and somewhere in there it occurred to me that I had begun curating my mother instead of visiting her.

Her laugh: two notes, the first high and startled, the second lower, like a gate swinging. She used to laugh at her own laugh, which doubled it. In March, Marisol — the aide, who does a little dance when a good song comes on — slipped on the kitchen rug mid-spin, and my mother laughed so hard she had to hold the counter, and I got all of it on video. In June she laughed at something I never saw. Maybe nothing. My phone came up out of my pocket before I had decided anything, and my mother looked at it, the little black rectangle between us, and asked, "Are we supposed to be doing something?"

"No," I said, and put it away, but the laugh was over. I did the math standing at the counter: four hundred videos of my mother laughing, and I had been present for almost none of them. I had been a witness, which is a person who stands slightly outside her own life, holding a rectangle.

Marisol told me once, wiping jam off my mother's chin, "She doesn't know what day it is, but she knows when you're in a hurry."

I had been in a hurry for six months.

In June a storm came through and took the power with it. No television, no lamps, the house gone dim and green the way it gets, the maples out front going wild. My mother sat at the window and watched them and said, "The trees are clapping." She was so pleased. My phone was charging in the kitchen, and I want to be honest: I thought about it. Then I sat down next to her and watched the trees clap.

After a while she began to hum. Not a song with words. The kitchen song, the wordless one she hummed my whole childhood while pots went on and off the stove. I hummed the next phrase without deciding to, and she patted my knee to keep time, and when it came around again she looked at me — not puzzled, not checking — and said, "There you are."

Not my name. Better than my name. *There you are.* As if she'd been keeping count of something else entirely, all along. As if the person was never lost. Only the word for her.

She said "Junebug" on a Tuesday. I was pouring coffee. She didn't look up from the crossword she can't do anymore, just said it — the name no one else has ever called me — the way you'd try an old key in a lock, to see if it still turned.

"Yes," I said. "Here I am."

I didn't reach for the notebook. I didn't get my phone. It may have been the last time; it may not have been. I've stopped keeping count. The notebook is in the kitchen drawer with the batteries and the dead pens, and I'm leaving it there. Some things I'll learn from the far side, like everybody does. And some I'll let be what they were that morning: not the last, not the first. Just a time. One of ours.

**The Words He Kept**

My father spent forty years on the radio. Farm reports, school closings, the Saturday swap shop, high school basketball when the regular man had laryngitis. His voice went into strangers' kitchens at six in the morning and told them about rain. People recognized him at the grocery store before they saw him — they'd hear him ask where the vinegar was and turn around. At home he was worse. He was a man who used forty words for vinegar. Dinner took two hours because every meal came with a story, every story had three endings, and he'd back up and take the second one. My mother set a timer once, as a joke. He talked through the buzzer.

He never once ran out of words. That's what I keep coming back to. Sixty-two years, and I never saw him reach for one and come back empty-handed.

The first one he lost was "collar." He called it the neck of the shirt, and we laughed, and he laughed, and it took us a year to understand it wasn't the start of a joke.

Then "avenue." Then the names of birds. Then "perhaps," which he had always used like salt. The neurologist had a word — aphasia — and a phrase — primary progressive — and a metaphor I have never forgiven: the brain is closing rooms. He said it the way a man describes weather.

I started the list at the hospital, on the back of a parking receipt. It began as a joke too: his words, the survivors. It stopped being a joke fast.

At first the losses looked random. They weren't. The fancy words went first, the ones he'd loved showing off — onomatopoeia, peninsula, hullabaloo. Then the abstractions. Justice. Loneliness. Tomorrow lasted longer than I would have guessed.

What stayed was concrete. The needed stuff, the daily bread of language — literally: bread stayed. Water stayed. Out. Keys. Door. The dog's name.

For a while he still talked the way he always had, full speed, no pauses, the old radio cadence — but the sentences had stopped carrying anything. "The morning took it over by the tomorrow," he'd say, comfortable, certain, and look to me for agreement. I agreed. I agreed with everything. That was the winter I learned that fluency is only the sound of language, not the thing itself. He could still say anything. He just couldn't mean it.

Some days he knew. Those were the days he didn't talk at all. He'd sit at the kitchen table with a crossword he could no longer fill in, snapping a pen against his thumb, snap, snap, snap, like a man tapping a wall to find the hollow place.

He tried once to tell me about his own father. Something important — he kept starting over, kept pointing at his chest. After ten minutes he stopped, patted my hand, and said, "Another day." We both knew. We said "another day" to each other for two years after that. It became our word for everything we couldn't say.

My mother had been gone eleven years. Her name — Eleanor — lasted longer than I expected. Longer than mine, at first. He'd see me come through the door and say "Eleanor," and I stopped correcting him sometime in March, because what was I correcting, exactly? Then in the fall I found him at the dresser holding her photograph, and he looked up at me, apologetic, and said, "June."

I'm June.

He never got Eleanor back. My name went everywhere after that. It did everything. It meant her, me, the whole category of women he had loved and trusted.

By the next year he had maybe sixty words. Then thirty. I moved the list from receipts into a notebook, because I finally understood what it was: a tide going out, and me marking the water line.

Here is some of what stayed:

Bread. Water. Door. Out. Wait. Yes. No. Petey. The word for cold. My name.

Petey the dog outlived Eleanor by two years in that mouth. I've made some peace with that. Mostly.

He lost "no" before "yes." I'm still thinking about what that means. Whatever else was being taken, he stayed a man who agreed with the world.

"Out" became a vocabulary of its own. He'd stand at the door in his coat saying it — out, out — and it could mean the yard, the street, the car, anywhere that wasn't this. We walked a lot that year. He pointed at things and I named them, and he'd nod like a farmer reading the sky.

I read to him at the end. He couldn't follow a plot and didn't need one. His face did the listening, leaning toward the sound the way it had always leaned — forty years of his voice going out into the dark, and now one coming back to him. I read him the farm report. Rain developing after midnight. He nodded like a man receiving good news.

The last winter, he had ten words. Nine of them were for asking. Water — and a glass appeared. Out — and there was the door, the coat, the snow, the two of us. Wait — wait. Wait.

The tenth was my name.

He spent it on everything. The blanket, the window, the soup, the light moving along the wall: "June," he'd say, pleased, presenting each thing to me like he'd found it, and in a way he had. I had stopped being a name and become his word for the entire category of good things. It is the most extravagant thing anyone has ever done with my name. Forty years on the radio, a man who never once ran out of words — and at the end, down to one, and the one was mine.

The last morning, it was snowing hard. He was looking past me at the window when he said it, and it wasn't a question and it wasn't a greeting. He said it the way he used to say rain developing after midnight. A man telling you what's coming. What's here. What's true.

"June," he said.

I know, I said. I know.

**Inventory**

Sixty-one coat hangers. June counted them twice, because that was the kind of arithmetic you did when you couldn't do anything else.

Her mother had been dead eleven days. The house had to be empty by the first of the month. Her brother, calling from Phoenix, said the thing there is to say: don't keep anything you'll have to dust. He meant it kindly. He was better at meaning things kindly from a distance. He'd offered to fly out; she'd told him not to; and this was a thing they would both go on pretending was practical.

So June counted. She counted because numbers didn't grieve. A number was a closed door, and she was grateful to it.

The kitchen yielded: twelve dinner plates, nine mugs (no two matching), forty-one forks, seventeen Tupperware lids against nine containers — a ratio that has never once in the history of the species come out even — and a button jar older than the house. She declined to count the drawer of rubber bands and twist ties. Some things want to stay wild.

The house was small and close to the road, the color of weak coffee. Her mother had lived in it for fifty-one years. June had grown up in it, then grown away, which is its own kind of arithmetic.

The basement: a salad spinner, a fondue set from a marriage that ended before June could walk, a box of ornaments labeled in her mother's hand — *angels: 4. broken angels: 3.* The broken ones kept. Her mother had kept the broken ones.

There were 214 books, and inside the books her mother's bookmarks: grocery receipts, a parking stub, a takeout menu folded to the coupon. The receipts were dated. One, from a hardware store, March 1996, marked a page forty pages from the end of a novel. June stood in the living room doing the math. Her mother had bought rope and seeds, and then stopped reading — or the receipt was simply the nearest flat thing. You couldn't know. That was the trouble with the dead. They left you the data and took the interpretation.

Her eyes went hot at the bookshelf, so she counted the bookshelf.

She priced everything for Saturday. She was good at this, the way people who are frightened of feelings are good at systems. Strangers would come and carry her mother's life out to their cars in reusable grocery bags. This was called settling an estate.

She saved the nightstand for last, the way she'd once eaten around the middle of a sandwich. In the drawer, under the TV remote and a magnifying glass, was a stack of index cards, held together by a rubber band from the kitchen drawer that had refused to be counted.

The cards were in her mother's handwriting. They were lists.

*June, 18 months. Words: 38. New this month: 11 — moon, spoon, gone, more, bird, no.*

June sat down on the edge of the bed, which still smelled like the bed.

*June, 5. Freckles: 9 (new: 2, left arm). Teeth out: 3.*

*June, 8. Height 4'2". Read 19 library books over the summer. Uses "antidisestablishment" to win arguments. Winning.*

*June, 11. Questions per day: approx. 200. Best one: "Do dogs know they're dogs?"*

*June, 15. Door slams: 4. Still my June.*

*June came. 26 hours. Flew through O'Hare. Luggage lost both ways.*

The cards went on for years, decades. Her mother had been counting her. All that time June had assumed she was being tolerated, or surveilled, or managed — and no. Her mother had stood at the edge of her life with a pencil, keeping watch, counting freckles like a jeweler counting stones.

Then the recent cards, the handwriting gone soft and large.

*Birds today: juncos 7, cardinal 1 (male), doves 2.*

*Juncos 9. No cardinal.*

*Rain. Birds 0. Quiet day. Called June — 12 minutes.*

June had no memory of a twelve-minute call. It had been a nothing call, a Tuesday. Are you eating. Yes. Are you. Yes. Twelve minutes, and her mother had written it down the way you write down treasure. She tried to remember where she'd been during those twelve minutes. Somewhere urgent. Probably her phone.

Outside, an actual bird crossed the actual yard, and June watched it go and did not know its name. Her mother would have known. Her mother had known the names of everything that visited.

She had thought the counting was her own invention — a trick for keeping grief off her, arithmetic as armor. It wasn't armor. It was inheritance. Her mother had counted because you cannot keep anything, not really — not a daughter's new words, not a freckle, not a Tuesday call — except by noticing it, and writing it down, and holding on. The numbers were never closed doors. They were doors held open, all those years, by a pencil.

Saturday came. The strangers came. A woman bought the fondue set and asked if it worked. It had never worked. June said yes. A man bought the salad spinner for a dollar and counted out the coins. Everyone, it turned out, was counting. The house emptied in reusable grocery bags.

What didn't sell was nothing that mattered, because June had already taken it: the cards, the button jar, the three broken angels.

At home, at her own kitchen table, she opened a fresh pack of index cards — she was her mother's daughter; this was the news of the week — and wrote the date. Then: *Mom's cards: 94. Read tonight: all. Times read: twice. Cried: yes. Fine.*

And below that, because a list has to start somewhere, because you cannot keep a thing except by counting it:

*Juncos at my feeder: 5.*

No cardinal yet. She was watching for it. The feeder was full. She had a pencil.

**Small Thunder**

The last mechanical cash register in the city rang for the final time on a Tuesday in March, and Nora was there to record it.

Mr. Alvi had run the hardware store for forty-one years. His last sale was a box of finishing nails, seventy-nine cents, marked down from a price he'd written by hand. He slid them across the counter and looked at the register the way you look at a horse you've decided not to sell after all. "Go on," he told her. "Do it again."

She didn't need asking twice. The drawer sprang with a sound like a bell struck inside a wooden box — the ka-ching everyone thinks they remember from old movies, except realer, thicker, with a rattle in the tail where the drawer bounced on its runners. She recorded it four more times. On the fifth, Mr. Alvi laid his hand flat on the brass top, and she caught the small stunned silence of that too.

This is her job, more or less. Nora archives vanishing sounds. Not the big ones — symphonies, speeches; others have those covered. The small ones. The coin return of the last payphone, which still advertised a pizza parlor in grease pencil. The dial-up modem's shriek, which she once described to a twelve-year-old as the sound of the internet clearing its throat. The clunk-and-roll of a vending machine delivering a can of root beer.

She has rules. She records in the wild when she can, because a typewriter is only a typewriter if someone is typing. She logs date, location, temperature — cold changes pitch — because sound is just air remembering what happened to it, and air cares about the weather.

The project started in her mother's kitchen. Or ended there — she's never sure which. Her mother was dying the way a house is demolished: slowly, then all at once. One afternoon she stood in that kitchen, heard the pressure cooker begin its hiss, and thought, absurdly: who will know what this sounded like? So she held up her phone. She got the cooker, the drawer with the loose runner, the faucet that needed a quarter-turn past sensible. The screen door took two tries, because the door was really two sounds — the slam, then the latch catching half a second later, like an echo with a job. And underneath it all, her mother humming in the next room. A song Nora still can't name.

Her mother died that October. Nora has forty-seven minutes of a kitchen. She has never played a second of it.

People find her. Mostly they want things she can get: church bells, milk bottles, a rotary phone dialed with a pencil. But last winter a man named Frank wrote about his wife's sewing machine. A treadle-powered Singer, 1919. He didn't want the machine, he said. He wanted *her* using it — the rhythm, the way she slowed at the ends of seams, the way when she stopped, the treadle did a little dying fall, "like a music box giving up." He'd tried humming it to his granddaughter; it came out wrong. He closed politely: *I know this isn't something you can record.*

He was right, and she tried anyway. She found a working Singer at an estate sale, oiled it, set a microphone by the treadle. It ran beautifully. It sounded like nothing. The mechanism was perfect, but the rhythm — the hesitations, the speed of a woman deciding — was gone, because it had never lived in the machine. It lived in Lorraine's foot. (Frank mentioned her name once, casually, the way you mention someone still in the room.) She recorded the empty machine anyway and sent it with a note about what was missing.

Frank wrote back the next morning. *That's not it,* he said. *But thank you. It's close enough to miss her by.*

She has that sentence pinned above her desk. The truest thing anyone has said about her profession. Every archive is a bet that the copy will carry some of the original, and every archivist knows it won't. You keep the jar, not the summer. You do it anyway.

Lately she's started recording things that aren't vanishing yet: her refrigerator at 3 a.m., the crowd at a little-league game, rain on her particular roof, which is not the same as rain on yours. A new phase of the project, or the end of her objectivity — she's decided it doesn't matter. Everything is the last of its kind if you wait long enough. The trick isn't catching things before they go. It's noticing they're here.

In September she drove out to a farm to record a woman canning tomatoes: lids into the kettle, tongs, the thick plop of fruit packed in glass. Then, as the kitchen cooled, the jars began to seal themselves one by one. Ping. Pause. Ping. Each lid sucking down tight, locking in August as well as it could.

The woman caught her expression. "My mother called that small thunder," she said.

Nora kept recording and thought: this is the whole archive. The entire impossible job. Not the keeping — the sound the keeping makes. Ping. Pause. Ping. Not lost; sealed.

Somewhere in her desk, a kitchen waits in the dark with its hand on the lid. Forty-seven minutes. The slam, the latch catching half a second behind, the humming underneath it all. She'll play it someday. Not yet. Some jars take years to cool, and you have to be standing in the kitchen to hear the thunder.

# Form the West

My father learned to text at seventy-three, and from that day forward he sent me exactly one kind of message. Weather.

"WINDY. FORM THE WEST."
"HOT. NO WIND. DOGS WOULDN'T MOVE."
"RAIN ALL NIGHT. GUTTER LOOSE AGAIN."

No questions, no answers, no sign-off. My sister-in-law taught him at the kitchen table, one enormous finger at a time, and his first message ever — to her — was "SUNNY. THANK YOU FOR THIS." I used to reply anyway. Did you fix the gutter? Are you eating? He never responded, not once, which my brother said proved the whole thing was just Dad's way of talking to us without having to talk to us. "He picks up when you call," my brother said. "He's not a mystery." But he was, a little. Rain or shine, the report came at six, his time. You don't send somebody the wind speed every evening for four years by accident.

So I learned to read them, and that took a while. "CLEAR. COLD. STARS OUT" meant he'd slept well and wanted somebody to know the sky was doing something worth seeing. "FOG ALL DAY. DIDN'T GO OUT" meant the fog was indoors too, if you understand me. "WIND SWITCHED ROUND TO THE EAST. SMELLS LIKE RAIN" meant rain by morning, and it always was. "HOT AGAIN. GARDEN'S DONE" meant he had decided to be at peace with it. When I finished my degree at thirty-six, he didn't say congratulations. He said, "PERFECT DAY. NOT ONE CLOUD." As far as I could tell from two states away, it was raining there. But I understood. It was a perfect day because I was in it.

Eventually I stopped asking questions and started answering. I'd send him my weather — "RAINING HERE TOO" — and he'd never acknowledge it, but the next evening's report might end with "RAIN STOPPING YOUR WAY SOON." It always did. I took that as evidence of receipt.

The year my marriage ended, he sent nothing for eleven days, which frightened me more than anything else that year. I called. He said the weather was "nothing worth reporting," the only weather lie he ever told. Then, on the twelfth day: "STORMS PASS. SOME SLOW." I sat on the floor of my half-empty apartment and read it forty times. It was the longest thing he ever sent me, and the only advice he ever gave me about anything, and it was accurate. It took three years. He never once asked how I was doing. He just kept sending the sky.

Some reports were for nobody but him, I think. Every October ninth: "RAIN. YOUR MOTHER WOULD HAVE LIKED IT." Fourteen years gone, and he still filed on her behalf. What she liked about rain, I never asked her, and I never asked him, and now there is no one left to ask.

Then, one June: "SNOWING. BIG FLAKES. FALLING SLOW."

I called him before I'd finished reading it. He sounded like always, low and unhurried, a man with time.

"Dad. It's June."

"Is it," he said. Not a question.

"Is it snowing there?"

"Were you born in June?" he said.

No. April. There'd been a freak storm the day I was born — my mother used to tell it, how the nurses carried me to the window and showed me the snow, as if the hospital had arranged it.

"Well," my father said, and I could hear the shrug. "That's the one I've got."

After that, his reports stopped coming from his sky and started coming from the archive. Some of the days I recognized. "HOT. DRY. FANS SOLD OUT EVERYWHERE" — the summer we hauled hay, me seventeen and sunburned. "RAIN, THEN SUN, THEN RAIN AGAIN." I asked about that one. "Day your mother said yes," he said. "Couldn't make up its mind."

I started calling every evening just before six, and asking, "What's the weather today, Dad?" And he'd give me a day with me in it. "CLEAR. COLD. GOOD DAY FOR A DRIVE." "Whose day is that?" "Day we took you to college. You cried the whole way." "I did not." "You did," he said. "Weather didn't hold it against you."

Once: "HAIL. LOUD ON THE SHED ROOF." Whose day, I asked. "Day you were due," he said. "Weather held you another week." And once: "SNOW AT SUNDOWN. PINK SNOW." Whose day. He was quiet long enough that I checked the call was still going. "First day I saw your mother," he said. "Snowed pink at sundown. Never told a soul." I sat down on my kitchen floor again — different floor, different grief.

The doctors had names for all of it. I didn't want the names. I wanted the forecasts.

His last text came on a Tuesday, and I want to tell you he knew, that he signed off, that it was something. It was: "CLEAR. CAN SEE FAR TODAY." Four days later my brother called me at work, and I already knew, the way you know weather.

We cleared the house in November. His phone was in the nightstand drawer, still charged, because somebody — my brother, probably — kept plugging it in, and neither of us could say why out loud. "You keep it," my brother said, and put it in my hand, which was as close as either of us came to saying what it was. On the last morning I stood on the porch at six and did the thing he always did: licked a finger, held it up. West. I know that trick the way I know a ring around the moon means something coming, the way I know which clouds are fair-weather clouds and which ones you watch. He taught me the sky for thirty years without once meaning to.

Then I typed: "CLEAR. WINDY. FORM THE WEST."

Form. My thumb did that on its own. I looked at it a long time and sent it anyway — to his number, from his porch.

Delivered, said the phone.

I knew better. But it was kind of it to say.
